event: Thirty-six countries and the European Union joined a special tribunal established to investigate and prosecute crimes of aggression related to Ukraine.

verified_facts.statement: Thirty-six countries and the European Union established a special tribunal to investigate and prosecute crimes of aggression related to Ukraine.
verified_facts.note: The International Crimes of Aggression Tribunal (ICAT) was formally established in 2023; exact membership roster confirmable via Council of Europe records.

verified_facts.statement: The tribunal was created outside the UN Security Council framework.
verified_facts.note: Established via Council of Europe mechanism, not UNSC resolution; this is structural fact.

verified_facts.statement: The United States did not join the tribunal and withdrew from the International Criminal Court Prosecutor's Agreement (ICPA) under the Trump administration.
verified_facts.note: US non-participation is documented; withdrawal timing and rationale are matters of record.

verified_facts.statement: The tribunal includes provisions for in absentia trials and immunity for sitting heads of state during their tenure.
verified_facts.note: Structural compromises are part of the founding statute; exact immunity scope requires statute review.

verified_facts.statement: The European Union committed €10 million in funding to the tribunal.
verified_facts.note: EU funding announcement is documented in Council statements.

verified_facts.statement: The tribunal has no independent enforcement mechanism (no police, arrest powers, or compulsory jurisdiction over non-member states).
verified_facts.note: Absence of enforcement apparatus is structural; relies on state cooperation for arrests.

verified_facts.statement: The Rome Statute was amended at Kampala in 2018 to make aggression prosecutable by the ICC.
verified_facts.note: Kampala amendments are historical fact; ICC aggression jurisdiction became operative in 2018.

verified_facts.statement: Russia is not a party to the tribunal and has not consented to its jurisdiction.
verified_facts.note: Russia's non-participation is documented; tribunal has no direct enforcement power over Russian territory.

unverified_shared_claims.statement: Over 150,000 crimes have been documented in Ukraine.
unverified_shared_claims.note: Cited by accountability framing; exact figure and methodology (what constitutes a 'documented crime') varies by source and requires verification against Ukrainian prosecutor records or UN fact-finding missions.

unverified_shared_claims.statement: The tribunal 'closes a critical gap' in international criminal law by being the first non-UNSC aggression tribunal.
unverified_shared_claims.note: Framing-dependent characterization; the ICC's Kampala amendments also address aggression, so 'first' and 'gap' are interpretive claims about institutional novelty.

unverified_shared_claims.statement: The tribunal will be dismissed as illegitimate by the Global South.
unverified_shared_claims.note: Predictive claim about reception; no polling or formal statement from Global South bloc confirms this as fact.

unverified_shared_claims.statement: The tribunal forecloses negotiated peace or serves as an obstacle to ceasefire.
unverified_shared_claims.note: Causal claim about diplomatic impact; no evidence yet of whether the tribunal's existence has materially affected peace negotiations.

unverified_shared_claims.statement: The tribunal signals European strategic autonomy from the United States.
unverified_shared_claims.note: Interpretive claim about geopolitical meaning; the fact of US non-participation is verified, but its significance for 'autonomy' is contested.

points_of_disagreement: Whether the tribunal represents legal innovation (Nuremberg trajectory) or institutional fragmentation (undermining the ICC and Rome Statute promise).
Whether immunity for sitting leaders is a pragmatic compromise enabling state participation or a fatal flaw that guarantees impunity for the architects of aggression.
Whether the tribunal serves justice for victims or is a 'legal spectacle' without enforcement teeth.
Whether the tribunal is legitimate international law or selective Western justice that undermines universality and ICC credibility in the Global South.
Whether the tribunal advances or obstructs peace by creating a permanent legal cloud over Russian leadership.
Whether US non-participation reflects Trump's geopolitical realignment toward Moscow or a principled position on institutional design.
Whether the tribunal demonstrates European autonomy or exposes European dependence on US enforcement capacity.
shared_foundation.summary: All framings accept that 36 countries and the EU created a special tribunal outside the UNSC to prosecute aggression crimes in Ukraine, that it includes in absentia trials and immunity for sitting leaders, that the US did not join, and that it lacks independent enforcement mechanisms. The disagreements concern whether these facts constitute legal progress or institutional failure, whether the tribunal serves justice or geopolitical selectivity, and whether it enables or obstructs peace.

framings.name: International Rule-of-Law Milestone
framings.question: Does this tribunal represent a historic advance in the international legal order?
framings.key_claim: The tribunal closes a critical gap in international criminal law by making the crime of aggression prosecutable for the first time outside the UN Security Council framework, completing a trajectory begun at Nuremberg.
framings.description: This framing presents the tribunal as a landmark development in international criminal law, filling the jurisdictional void left by the ICC's inability to try non-Rome-Statute states for the crime of aggression. It situates the tribunal in the arc from Nuremberg to the Rome Statute and positions it as a structural upgrade to global governance.
framings.emphasizes: Legal innovation, the Nuremberg precedent, UN Charter enforcement, deterrence of future aggressors, the historic novelty of a non-UNSC-created aggression tribunal
framings.downplays: Practical obstacles to enforcement, the absence of the US, questions about selectivity, and the immunity compromise for the 'troika'
sample_headlines: 'Point of no return': 36 countries join special tribunal to prosecute Vladimir Putin
Ukraine and the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression: Redefining International Justice

carriers.name: Council of Europe (official body)
carriers.excerpt: The tribunal will reaffirm the fundamental principle that war must not be waged as a tool of state policy.
carriers.role_evidence: The Council of Europe is the treaty-founding institution of the tribunal and the primary institutional proponent of this framing in official documentation.

carriers.name: Just Security (Dr. Iryna Mudra)
carriers.excerpt: The STCA seeks to close one of the most enduring gaps in international criminal law.
carriers.role_evidence: Ukraine's Deputy Head of the Presidential Office authored an op-ed for Just Security framing the tribunal as completing the Nuremberg-to-ICC trajectory.

carriers.name: Euronews
carriers.excerpt: 'Point of no return' in the search for justice.
carriers.role_evidence: Flagship European news outlet broadcast the 'point of no return' framing widely, drawing directly on official statements.

carriers.name: Chris Goebel / Public International Law & Policy Group (via Wikipedia citation)
carriers.excerpt: The first formal international tribunal for the crime of aggression created independently of the United Nations Security Council.
carriers.role_evidence: Legal expert foregrounded the structural novelty of the tribunal's independence from UNSC, amplifying the rule-of-law milestone framing in expert commentary.

carriers.name: Yale Journal of International Law (Wenaweser & Alavi)
carriers.excerpt: The frontiers of international criminal law are not fixed.
carriers.role_evidence: Yale JCIL piece authored by key Core Group negotiators provided the foundational scholarly articulation of this framing.

carriers.name: European Parliament
carriers.excerpt: The EU has repeatedly reaffirmed its strong commitment to ensuring full accountability for war crimes.
carriers.role_evidence: The European Parliament adopted a formal resolution endorsing the tribunal as an accountability mechanism, giving this framing institutional legislative weight.

framings.name: Accountability for Victims / Human Cost
framings.question: Does this tribunal deliver meaningful justice for the millions of Ukrainians harmed by the invasion?
framings.key_claim: The tribunal is a concrete mechanism for the millions of Ukrainian victims to see the architects of their suffering held personally and criminally responsible.
framings.description: This framing centers the Ukrainian civilian experience — displacement, deaths, abducted children, destroyed infrastructure — and asks whether the tribunal translates political momentum into felt justice for real people. It is often articulated by Ukrainian officials, civil society, and human rights organizations.
framings.emphasizes: Victims' needs and participation, the human scale of harm, the over-150,000 documented crimes, the Register of Damages, and the tribunal's role in empowering survivors
framings.downplays: Jurisdictional technicalities, geopolitical coalition management, the long timeline before any verdict
sample_headlines: Justice for the crime of aggression — the Special Tribunal must put Ukrainian victims center stage
36 Countries and EU Back Special Tribunal to Prosecute Putin for Crime of Aggression

carriers.name: Kyiv Independent (op-ed)
carriers.excerpt: The Tribunal can still deliver justice to millions — but the Council of Europe must ensure that Ukrainian victims... are central to every stage.
carriers.role_evidence: Published a direct advocacy piece demanding victim-centricity, positioning the tribunal's human-cost dimension as the primary measure of its success.

carriers.name: Amnesty International / FIDH / ICJ (joint statement)
carriers.excerpt: The Tribunal must not shy away from seeking indictments against all those who ordered, planned and implemented the crime of aggression.
carriers.role_evidence: Joint NGO statement published ahead of the tribunal's formal adoption demanded victim-centered design features, amplifying this framing in the human rights community.

carriers.name: Kyiv Post
carriers.excerpt: The tribunal aims to fill a legal gap by targeting those responsible for planning and launching Russia's full-scale invasion.
carriers.role_evidence: Widely-read English-language Ukrainian outlet framed the tribunal primarily through the lens of restoring justice for Ukraine's population.

carriers.name: Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha
carriers.excerpt: The moral foundation of Europe and the world will only be restored when the crime of aggression against Ukraine is punished.
carriers.role_evidence: Ukraine's top diplomat delivered this framing at the formal adoption ceremony, giving it official state-level articulation.

carriers.name: Human Rights First
carriers.excerpt: International justice can be rendered ineffective by immunity or the unwillingness of states to cooperate.
carriers.role_evidence: Human rights NGO published explainer foregrounding victim harm and the tribunal's potential to deliver accountability for Ukrainian civilians.

framings.name: Legal Viability and Enforcement Skepticism
framings.question: Can this tribunal actually prosecute and convict anyone, given immunity rules and the absence of the accused?
framings.key_claim: The tribunal's structural compromises — immunity for the 'troika' while in office, in absentia trials, and the absence of any enforcement mechanism — may render it an expensive legal spectacle rather than effective justice.
framings.description: This framing questions the operational credibility of the tribunal, focusing on unresolved legal problems: sovereign immunity for sitting heads of state, the novelty and potential unconstitutionality of its jurisdictional claims, in absentia proceedings, and the near-zero prospect of actually arresting Putin or other senior Russian officials.
framings.emphasizes: The immunity compromise, in absentia proceedings, absence of enforcement, unresolved questions about the tribunal's 'international character', funding uncertainties
framings.downplays: The symbolic and deterrence value of the tribunal, its evidence-preservation function, and political momentum behind it
sample_headlines: Building a Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine (EJIL: Talk!)
A Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression Against Ukraine: Origins, Debates, and Implications (Yale JCIL)

carriers.name: EJIL: Talk! (European Journal of International Law blog)
carriers.excerpt: Existing jurisprudence has offered only limited and, at times, internally inconsistent guidance on the interaction between international or hybrid tribunals and the personal immunities of sitting heads of state.
carriers.role_evidence: Leading international law blog provided the earliest sustained scholarly analysis of the immunity paradox and jurisdictional limitations, originating this framing in academic discourse.

carriers.name: Opinio Juris (Dr. Andrew Forde)
carriers.excerpt: If a Special Tribunal only focuses on a small group of elite prosecutions, at a tremendous cost and with no guarantee of ever apprehending let alone convicting these suspects, what does this do for individual justice?
carriers.role_evidence: Dublin City University law scholar raised the enforcement-gap critique prominently, amplifying skepticism among international law practitioners.

carriers.name: Amnesty International (joint statement)
carriers.excerpt: The possibility of holding trials in absentia also marks a regressive development from previously established international criminal tribunals.
carriers.role_evidence: Human rights coalition publicly criticized the immunity and in absentia provisions, bringing legal-viability skepticism to a mass human rights audience.

carriers.name: Euronews
carriers.excerpt: The court will face limitations in bringing Putin to justice.
carriers.role_evidence: Included enforcement skepticism as a counterpoint note in its otherwise celebratory coverage of the tribunal's founding.

carriers.name: Yale Journal of International Law (Wenaweser & Alavi)
carriers.excerpt: This hybrid character raises a fundamental and unresolved legal question: at what point does a regional tribunal attain sufficient international character to fully override personal immunities?
carriers.role_evidence: Insider account by Core Group negotiators acknowledged the immunity compromise openly, framing the viability question as the tribunal's central unresolved challenge.

framings.name: Selective Justice / Western Double Standard
framings.question: Does the tribunal apply international law equally, or does it reflect Western power rather than universal principle?
framings.key_claim: A tribunal created by and for Western-aligned states to prosecute only Russian officials constitutes selective justice that undermines the universality of international criminal law and will be dismissed as illegitimate by the Global South.
framings.description: This framing challenges the tribunal's principled neutrality by asking why similar mechanisms do not exist for US actions in Iraq, Israeli actions in Gaza, or other situations. It is articulated by international law critics, Global South-aligned commentators, and the first ICC Chief Prosecutor, and is actively amplified in Russian state messaging.
framings.emphasizes: US hypocrisy (not being an ICC member, shaping Rome Statute to protect itself), the absence of similar tribunals for other aggressors, Global South non-participation, the gap between Gaza accountability and Ukraine accountability
framings.downplays: The specific and documented nature of the invasion, the legal arguments for why the Ukraine case is distinct, the voluntary withdrawal of the US from the process
sample_headlines: Ending Selective Justice for the International Crime of Aggression (Just Security, Luis Moreno Ocampo)
A New Court to Prosecute Russia's Illegal War? (International Crisis Group)

carriers.name: Luis Moreno Ocampo / Just Security
carriers.excerpt: The proposals to create an ad hoc tribunal to potentially prosecute President Vladimir Putin for the commission of the crime of aggression promotes nothing short of selective justice.
carriers.role_evidence: The founding Chief Prosecutor of the ICC authored the most prominent early articulation of the selective justice critique, giving it mainstream international law credibility.

carriers.name: International Crisis Group
carriers.excerpt: The selective justice critique – which hits home in many Global South countries – will be particularly stinging.
carriers.role_evidence: Prominent conflict-resolution think tank gave the selectivity framing policy-community reach, explicitly linking it to Global South reservations.

carriers.name: Oxford Academic / Journal of Conflict and Security Law
carriers.excerpt: The third major criticism of the proposed tribunal is that it would amount to selective justice, which would undermine the broader international criminal justice project.
carriers.role_evidence: Peer-reviewed legal journal article systematically catalogued the selectivity critique as one of the 'three major criticisms' of the tribunal, cementing it in academic discourse.

carriers.name: Scientific Research Publishing / SCIRP (comparative ICC study)
carriers.excerpt: A comparative examination of Palestine and Ukraine to critically investigate the ICC's alleged selective application of international justice.
carriers.role_evidence: Academic comparison of ICC treatment of Ukraine vs. Palestine amplified the double-standard framing by grounding it in comparative case-study methodology.

carriers.name: Yale Journal of International Law (Wenaweser & Alavi)
carriers.excerpt: The positions taken by some major States from the Global South... were often justified by reference to concerns about selective enforcement of international law.
carriers.role_evidence: Insider negotiators acknowledged Global South selectivity concerns explicitly within their own supportive account, lending the framing credibility even from pro-tribunal voices.

framings.name: US Disengagement / Trump Geopolitical Realignment
framings.question: What does US withdrawal from the tribunal process signal about the future of Western-led international institutions and Ukraine peace prospects?
framings.key_claim: The Trump administration's withdrawal from the ICPA and refusal to join the tribunal exposes a fundamental US-Europe rift and signals that Washington is prioritizing rapprochement with Moscow over accountability for aggression.
framings.description: This framing treats the tribunal not primarily as a legal story but as a barometer of transatlantic fracture and Trump's foreign policy pivot toward Russia. It focuses on the US withdrawal from the ICPA, the absence of US funding, and the tension between the tribunal's existence and Trump's amnesty-floating peace proposals.
framings.emphasizes: The US withdrawal, budget gaps, Trump peace plan vs. tribunal purpose, the shift from Biden to Trump accountability postures, the Europe-goes-it-alone narrative
framings.downplays: The legal substance of the tribunal, the momentum among the 36 participating countries, the possibility that accountability and peace talks can proceed in parallel
sample_headlines: US to Withdraw from Group Investigating Putin for Crimes Against Ukraine, NYT Reports
US to Pull Out of Task Force Probing Russian Aggression in Ukraine (Newsweek)

carriers.name: New York Times (via Kyiv Independent / Newsweek reporting)
carriers.excerpt: The U.S. has privately told European officials that it is pulling back from an international group investigating Russian leaders for the crime of aggression.
carriers.role_evidence: NYT broke the US withdrawal story, originating the framing that tied the tribunal's fate to Trump-era foreign policy realignment.

carriers.name: Newsweek
carriers.excerpt: Withdrawing from it is likely to be seen as the latest indication of the Trump administration's move away from Biden's push to make Putin personally accountable.
carriers.role_evidence: Newsweek provided the mass-audience amplification of the US-withdrawal story, explicitly framing it as a Biden-to-Trump accountability reversal.

carriers.name: Euronews
carriers.excerpt: The lack of US engagement under President Donald Trump has previously raised concerns about budgetary shortfalls.
carriers.role_evidence: Euronews embedded the US disengagement framing into its main tribunal coverage, keeping it live for a European audience.

carriers.name: Human Rights First
carriers.excerpt: Although the United States helped form the 'core group' that developed the Special Tribunal, the Trump administration withdrew from this effort in March 2025.
carriers.role_evidence: Civil society explainer explicitly foregrounded US withdrawal as a defining feature of the tribunal's political landscape.

carriers.name: Opinio Juris (Dr. Andrew Forde)
carriers.excerpt: Such questions are all the more prominent now that the US Administration is pursuing an irrational, deeply protectionist and dangerous approach to international relations.
carriers.role_evidence: Legal scholar situated the US withdrawal within a broader critique of Trump foreign policy, amplifying the geopolitical-realignment framing in expert commentary.

framings.name: Peace Process Obstruction
framings.question: Does the tribunal entrench the conflict by making a negotiated settlement politically impossible?
framings.key_claim: By creating a permanent legal cloud over Putin and the Russian leadership, the tribunal forecloses any negotiated exit from the war and may serve as an obstacle to the ceasefire deal that would stop the killing.
framings.description: This framing, associated with Trump administration messaging and pro-settlement analysts, argues that prosecutorial processes and peace processes are in tension. It points to the 28-point Trump draft peace proposal that floated blanket amnesty, and to the logic that Putin will not negotiate if conviction is the only end-state on offer.
framings.emphasizes: Ceasefire urgency, the costs of continued fighting, the need for off-ramps for Russian leadership, the tribunal as a diplomatic dead-end
framings.downplays: The deterrence value of accountability, Ukrainian and European insistence that justice and peace are complementary, the documented scale of Russian war crimes
sample_headlines: Trump's push for a peace deal has cast doubt over the tribunal's core purpose
Trump's latest Ukraine peace proposal sparks strong Republican reaction (Atlantic Council)

carriers.name: Euronews (citing Trump draft peace proposal)
carriers.excerpt: Trump's push for a peace deal between Ukraine and Russia has also cast doubt over the tribunal's core purpose.
carriers.role_evidence: Euronews acknowledged the peace-obstruction tension as a journalistic counterpoint, reflecting its circulation in diplomatic discourse.

carriers.name: Trump Administration (via NYT/Newsweek reporting on ICPA withdrawal)
carriers.excerpt: The move underscores the foreign policy shift in Washington as the Trump administration seeks to restore ties with Moscow while pushing for a swift peace deal.
carriers.role_evidence: The Trump administration's ICPA withdrawal operationalized the peace-obstruction framing as US policy, the clearest institutional adoption of this narrative.

carriers.name: Atlantic Council
carriers.excerpt: Those who think pressuring the victim and appeasing the aggressor will bring peace are kidding themselves.
carriers.role_evidence: The Atlantic Council foregrounded Republican Congressional pushback against Trump's peace-over-accountability approach, functioning as a direct critic of this framing.

carriers.name: New Eastern Europe
carriers.excerpt: Each proposal... serves as a tool for power redistribution rather than a genuine end to the war.
carriers.role_evidence: Eastern European analysis journal pushed back against the peace-first framing by historicizing failed peace proposals as instruments of Russian leverage.

framings.name: ICC Fragmentation / Institutional Architecture Debate
framings.question: Does creating yet another ad hoc tribunal weaken the ICC and fragment the international criminal justice system?
framings.key_claim: Establishing a special tribunal outside the ICC risks permanently fragmenting the international criminal justice system and undermines the promise made at Rome in 1998 that a permanent court would make ad hoc tribunals obsolete.
framings.description: This framing, dominant in international law scholarship, argues that the correct response to the ICC's jurisdictional gap would be to fix the Rome Statute rather than create a parallel institution. It raises concerns about institutional duplication, resource competition, inconsistent jurisprudence, and the signal sent to future states considering joining the ICC.
framings.emphasizes: The fragmentation risk, the Rome Statute Kampala amendments as the proper fix, the ICC's existing Ukraine mandate, institutional coherence, and precedent-setting dangers
framings.downplays: The political impossibility of amending the Rome Statute given Russia's veto, the urgency of prosecuting the crime of aggression now, and the tribunal's explicit complementarity clause
sample_headlines: Ending Selective Justice for the International Crime of Aggression (Just Security)
The Road Not (Yet) Taken: A Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression Against Ukraine (Opinio Juris)

carriers.name: Luis Moreno Ocampo / Just Security
carriers.excerpt: Fixing the statute of the International Criminal Court rather than erecting an ad hoc tribunal is the best approach.
carriers.role_evidence: The founding ICC Chief Prosecutor explicitly argued for ICC reform over ad hoc fragmentation, originating the institutional architecture framing.

carriers.name: Amnesty International / FIDH / ICJ (joint statement)
carriers.excerpt: Cases of aggression should normally be investigated and adjudicated by the ICC, and Rome Statute States Parties should ratify the Kampala amendment.
carriers.role_evidence: Human rights coalition simultaneously backed the tribunal while advocating for ICC primacy, amplifying the fragmentation concern in the human rights community.

carriers.name: Yale Journal of International Law (Wenaweser & Alavi)
carriers.excerpt: There was the concern that establishing a Special Tribunal might be perceived as undermining the ICC and weakening the promise made at the time of the creation of the ICC in 1998.
carriers.role_evidence: Core Group negotiators themselves described this ICC-fragmentation concern as a primary hesitation during the tribunal's design phase.

carriers.name: Opinio Juris (Dr. Andrew Forde)
carriers.excerpt: Some may argue that the pursuit of this initiative serves only to further undermine the International Criminal Court which is under enormous duress at present.
carriers.role_evidence: Opinio Juris piece foregrounded the fragmentation risk as a central policy question, amplifying the debate in practitioner legal communities.

carriers.name: House of Commons Library (UK Parliament research briefing)
carriers.excerpt: The most suitable and legally-sound avenue to establishing this is the subject of ongoing considerable debate among experts.
carriers.role_evidence: UK parliamentary research service flagged the institutional architecture debate as live and unresolved, bringing it into legislative-advisory discourse.

framings.name: European Autonomy / Geopolitical Resolve
framings.question: Does this tribunal demonstrate that Europe can lead on security and rule-of-law issues independently of the United States?
framings.key_claim: The tribunal's adoption by 36 countries through the Council of Europe — without the United States — signals a new phase of European strategic and legal autonomy in confronting Russian aggression.
framings.description: This framing, prominent in European institutional and political commentary, reads the tribunal as evidence of European agency rather than just an international justice story. It emphasizes that Europe acted despite US withdrawal, that the EU committed €10 million, and that the coalition includes non-European states like Australia and Costa Rica.
framings.emphasizes: European institutional leadership, US absence as a test of European self-reliance, the Council of Europe's role, non-European participation (Australia, Costa Rica), the EU's €10M funding commitment
framings.downplays: The 12 Council of Europe members that did not join (Hungary, Slovakia, Serbia, Turkey), practical enforcement limitations, and the need for broader non-Western buy-in
sample_headlines: 36 countries approve creation of special Ukraine tribunal to prosecute Russia (France 24)
Special tribunal for Russia gains major backing from European countries (RBC-Ukraine)

carriers.name: Council of Europe Secretary General Alain Berset
carriers.excerpt: Action now needs to be taken to follow up on this political commitment by securing the tribunal's functioning and funding.
carriers.role_evidence: Berset's public statements at the adoption ceremony foregrounded European institutional leadership as the story's organizing principle.

carriers.name: France 24
carriers.excerpt: Thirty-four European states – along with Australia and Costa Rica – said Friday they would join a proposed special tribunal for Ukraine.
carriers.role_evidence: Major French international broadcaster framed the coalition composition (34 European + 2 non-European) as the headline fact, emphasizing the European-led coalition character.

carriers.name: Moldovan President Maia Sandu
carriers.excerpt: The pressure on Russia must not abate. Support for Ukraine requires much more than financial aid — accountability for the crimes committed is also essential.
carriers.role_evidence: As the host of the Council of Europe session, Sandu's framing of accountability as a European political imperative amplified the European-autonomy narrative from a smaller state's perspective.

carriers.name: European Parliament (resolution B10-0211/2026)
carriers.excerpt: The EU has repeatedly reaffirmed its strong commitment to ensuring full accountability for war crimes.
carriers.role_evidence: The EP resolution formally endorsed the tribunal as a European institutional project, giving the European-autonomy framing its highest legislative expression.

carriers.name: Just Security (Dr. Iryna Mudra)
carriers.excerpt: Every additional state that joins the EPA strengthens the legitimacy, universality, and deterrent power of the STCA.
carriers.role_evidence: Ukraine's Presidential Office Deputy Head used the Just Security platform to call for broader non-European participation, implicitly centering Europe's leadership role as the current foundation.

gap_analysis: Missing are framings centered on: (1) Russia's counter-narrative and legitimacy claims regarding the tribunal's jurisdiction and impartiality, including Moscow's perspective on what constitutes aggression; (2) the practical resource and capacity constraints of smaller nations joining the tribunal, and burden-sharing equity concerns; (3) the tension between transitional justice goals and reconciliation/reconstruction needs in Ukraine itself; (4) perspectives from Global South countries not joining, including concerns about precedent-setting for their own conflicts or skepticism about selective enforcement against non-Western powers.

coverage_lean.event: Thirty-six countries and the European Union joined a special tribunal established to investigate and prosecute crimes of aggression related to Ukraine.
coverage_lean.skew: insufficient rated coverage to judge skew (DB is US-centric; many carriers unrated)

coalition.structure_note: 9 of 26 actors actively champion more than one framing (real cross-cutting, not just broad coverage); see the bridges and any contested actors for who connects — or splits — which lenses.
